paras: The sale of Charles Green under the Colorado vagrancy law took place in Leadville, Colorado, in late November 1880, when Green, a young Black man arrested as a vagrant, was auctioned off to labor for three months. The chief of police sold him for two dollars to C. E. Wyman, and a few days later Green was jailed on a theft charge and kept from his buyer. Papers in New Mexico and Indiana carried the story, the Indianapolis account presenting it as the return of something "old" under a new name.

According to an account drawn from the Leadville Carbonate Weekly Chronicle of November 27, 1880, a Colorado statute allowed a vagrant to be sold for a set period, with the auction proceeds paying the costs of the court case. Green, described as about twenty years old and as having "no visible means of support," was said to be the first man arrested as a vagrant in Leadville since it became a city.

Green was sentenced to be sold to labor for three months. At ten o'clock in the morning, E. H. Watson, the chief of police and a deputy sheriff, held the auction in front of Justice McDowall's office, and C. E. Wyman won it as the highest bidder at two dollars. Immediately after the sale, someone offered Wyman twenty dollars for Green's services, which he refused, saying he "was no slave broker."

A few days later Green was arrested again, charged with stealing two overcoats, boots, shoes and other goods worth about $100 before his first arrest. Unable to give $300 bail, he was lodged in the county jail to await court action, without Wyman's knowledge. When Wyman learned where Green was and demanded him, the officers refused; no report of the outcome of the theft case was found.

The Las Vegas Morning Gazette of New Mexico reported the sale on November 30 in a single line of its "Mountains and Plains" column, calling Green "a worthless negro" who had been "sold in Leadville under the vagrant act." The item ran between notes on Colorado water works and the weather, with no comment.

The fuller account appeared on December 11 in The Indianapolis Leader, in a "Cleveland, O., Items" column that retold the Leadville Chronicle's story under the line "Something old put in a new light." Its writer called Leadville "that benighted place," referred to Wyman as "the man who purchased him," and closed on the officers' refusal to give up "his man Green." The same page carried items on colored newspapers, Southern violence against Black people and a call for a Black cabinet appointment, placing the Leadville sale among race news rather than regional briefs.
The two papers named the man differently, the Las Vegas brief as "Charley Green" and the Indianapolis account, which drew on the Leadville paper, as Charles Green.

bases: Green, a Black man arrested as a vagrant, was sentenced to be sold to labor for three months and was auctioned by the chief of police to a private bidder (A1, A2).
Two papers with different wording agree that Green was sold in Leadville under the vagrant law (A1, A2), though both likely rest on Leadville press reports and only A2 gives details.
